sections.lever checks:
- Family and target: author B's i01 (notes/hooks.md, origin claude), sketch i02, written up word for word after its quick test (user, 2026-10-14, "both survived"). Match then exclude, with the exclusion in another paper: Doc 7's table marks only Australia and Finland as subnational, and Doc 9 shows Argentina's surveys were regional. Target medium; hard is also open (user: no Easy slot, "target medium and high"). Medium shows one slot, and every run on a "Medium 0/1" set on 2026-10-14 started at the High level, so the audit is against the high solver. Measured result pending.
- Dependency plan: Doc 7 Table 1 urine rows -> its footnote marks (Victoria, Finnish regions out) -> Doc 9 Table 2 and discussion (Argentina regional, out) -> largest remaining pair Turkey 18.0 -> 15.0 g -> 3.0 / 18.0 = 16.7%.
- Universe: Doc 7's eleven 24-hour urine rows (its text: "11 countries reported changes using 24-hour urine samples"), recomputed by script: Finland North Karelia women 28.85% and men 26.36%, Southwestern Finland women 18.68% and men 15.52%, Kuopio area 8.65% and 8.40% (all marked subnational); Argentina 17.86% (regional, Doc 9); Turkey 16.67%; Italy women 13.25% and men 12.26%; Fiji 11.97%; Slovenia men 9.79% and women 2.73%; United Kingdom 7.41%; Netherlands women 6.33% and men 2.02%; Victoria 1.27% (marked); Samoa and Switzerland rises. Outside Doc 7: Doc 3's UK "15% reduction in 24-h urinary sodium by 2011" (whole-country, smaller); Doc 3's NZ urine studies (convenience samples); Doc 8's Africa-Predict cohort (aged 20-30, no baseline level); Doc 9's Mongolia (24-hour urine 2011, spot urine 2019) and South Africa (one 2015 survey): no qualifying pair.
- Necessity (delete and guess, 2026-10-14): without Doc 9, no document describes Argentina's survey coverage, Doc 7 leaves its row unmarked, and a solver answers 17.9%. Without Doc 7, there are no country pairs in grams: Doc 3's UK 15% is the only whole-country urine fall, so a solver answers 15% (Doc 2 gives Turkey only as a "1.2g/day" sodium reduction with no level; pairing it with a recalled Turkish 2008 level of about 18 g would reach 16.7%: low risk, recorded). Closed book: no route to 16.7 without the table.
- Step audit (2026-10-14): (1) the 24-hour urine rows: pointed ("24-hour urine"); (2) the marked subnational rows: pointed ("whole-country", with the footnote in the same table); (3) Argentina left out: half-pointed: no question word names Argentina or its survey and its row carries no mark, but "whole-country" invites a coverage check and a search for Argentina or "regional" reaches Doc 9; (4) percentage to one decimal: pointed. One half-pointed step. The quick test (easier solver) did not clear it, which says nothing yet about the medium or high solver; the sibling bundle aq-04819's one partly unpointed step (a figure behind a second document) was cleared by the high model 3 of 3 the same day.
- Selected-lever checks: Match, then exclude: without the Doc 9 exclusion the answer is 17.9% (Argentina), recomputed 2.0 / 11.2 = 17.857%. Without the footnote: 28.8% (North Karelia women). Without the method condition: 26.5% (South Korea, dietary survey). State the rounding: Doc 7 prints Turkey's fall as "-17%", and the asked one decimal gives 16.7%, so copying the printed figure gives 17.0%, a different answer.
- Targeted failure modes: Wrong jurisdiction or scope / Misapplies a rule or premise: wrong answer 17.9% (Argentina's regional pair kept). It is the answer the easiest reading gives; not yet observed in a run. Considered and not declared: the printed rounding (17%), which "one decimal place" already rules out; the Finnish regions (28.8%), which the table itself marks.
- Calculation verification: author arithmetic, then Python Decimal (2026-10-14): 18.0 - 15.0 = 3.0; 3.0 / 18.0 = 0.166667 -> 16.7% (half up at one decimal); Argentina 2.0 / 11.2 = 17.857% -> 17.9%. Units: grams of salt a day; the fall is relative to the first survey.
- Semantic/ID/overview probes: "24-hour urine" or "24-h urine" reaches Doc 7's table and text, Doc 9 (Table 1, Table 2, discussion), Doc 3 (NZ convenience studies, UK 15%), Doc 8 (Africa-Predict) and Doc 1 (Land et al. meta-analysis); "regional" reaches Doc 9's Argentina entries; "national" reaches Doc 9's Mongolia and South Africa entries. No document prints 16.7 or names a largest whole-country fall. Shortest route: Doc 7's table and footnote, then a coverage check of Argentina in Doc 9.
- Precision/readings (each still possible; the words that reject it): (1) 17.9%: Argentina kept because its row is unmarked; rejected by "whole-country" through Doc 9. (2) 28.8% and the other Finnish regions, 1.3% Victoria: rejected by "whole-country" (marked in Doc 7). (3) 26.5% South Korea, 22.9% China, 19.3% Lithuania, 18.8% Canada: rejected by "24-hour urine". (4) 17% or 17.0%: Turkey's printed rounding; rejected by "one decimal place". (5) 3.0 g or 3.5 g: absolute falls; rejected by "percentage". (6) 15% UK (Doc 3): qualifies, smaller. (7) Sex-specific rows (Italy women 13.3%): not a country's mean, and smaller. (8) "cannot be determined": a strict solver could doubt that any unmarked row is whole-country; Doc 7 marks only Australia and Finland as subnational, and Doc 2 calls Turkey's reduction one "across an entire population". (9) Argentina's 2015 survey coverage: Doc 9 says Argentina's 24-hour urine surveys were regional and its baseline was not national, so the pair fails "two whole-country surveys" either way.
- Completeness: complete capture, no gaps (notes/intake.json); all ten documents read in full. Doc 7's Table 1 is complete (25 countries, matching "25/96" in its text); its missing figures and Supplemental Table 2 do not bear on these rows.
- Style/set review: 22 words, one ask, one number, precision stated; no cue clause; no file names; "whole-country" chosen over "national" so that the wording does not match Doc 9's "national measure" sentence. Set: q01 reads the same Doc 7 table (Argentina row) with a different lever and answer; neither gives the other's answer away.

sections.question: What is the largest percentage fall in a country's mean salt intake between two whole-country 24-hour urine surveys? Answer to one decimal place.
sections.reasoning:
Step 1. Source input (Doc 7, table of countries with reported data on change in mean salt intake): the rows whose assessment method is 24-hour urine are Argentina, Australia, Fiji, Finland, Italy, the Netherlands, Samoa, Slovenia, Switzerland, Turkey and the United Kingdom.
Step 2. Source input (Doc 7, same table and its footnote): the Australian row (Victoria) and the Finnish rows (Kuopio area, North Karelia, Southwestern Finland) carry the mark for "Change in salt intake measured at the subnational level", so they are not pairs of whole-country surveys. The other urine rows carry no mark.
Step 3. Source input (Doc 7, Argentina row): mean salt intake fell from 11.2 g a day to 9.2 g a day, the largest fall among the unmarked urine rows.
Step 4. Source input (Doc 9, surveillance table and discussion): Argentina's salt intake measurement by this method is listed as a "Regional survey", the discussion says "Argentina and South Africa conducted regional surveys to measure salt intake using 24-h urines", and only Mongolia had a national measure by this method at baseline. So Argentina's urine pair in Doc 7 is not a pair of whole-country surveys, and it is left out.
Step 5. Source input (Doc 7, Turkey row): mean salt intake fell from 18.0 g a day to 15.0 g a day; the row carries no subnational mark.
Step 6. Calculation (Doc 7): 18.0 - 15.0 = 3.0 (Turkey's fall in grams of salt a day, derived).
Step 7. Calculation (Doc 7): 3.0 / 18.0 = 16.7% (Turkey's fall as a share of its first survey's intake, derived and expressed as a percentage).
Step 8. Source input (Doc 7, remaining unmarked urine rows): Fiji, Italy, the Netherlands, Samoa, Slovenia, Switzerland and the United Kingdom all show smaller falls than Turkey's, or rises.
Step 9. Final answer (Doc 7 and Doc 9): the largest fall between two whole-country 24-hour urine surveys is Turkey's, 16.7% to one decimal place.
sections.targeted failure modes:
### Failure mode 1
Trap: Wrong jurisdiction or scope
How a careless solver fails: Misapplies a rule or premise

Why these are traps: Wrong jurisdiction or scope: Doc 7's salt-intake table lists Argentina's 24-hour urine pair, 11.2 to 9.2 g, without a subnational mark, so a careless solver answers 17.9%. Doc 9 says Argentina's urine surveys were regional; the largest whole-country pair left, Turkey's 18.0 to 15.0 g, gives 16.7%.
